channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Indonesia's benchmark stock index closed down 3.6% on 19 October after an 11.6% fall on Friday, which the Globe and Mail says is steeper than any two-session fall in 1998, after MSCI said it is considering reclassifying Indonesia.
item.description:
The Globe and Mail reports that Indonesia's benchmark stocks closed down 3.6% on 19 October after plunging 11.6% on Friday, a combined two-session fall it says is steeper than any during the 1998 Asian financial crisis, and that the index touched a six-year low during the session. The selling began after MSCI said it was considering shifting Indonesia to standalone status from emerging-market status, a move the Globe and Mail calls more severe than expected. LiveMint reports that foreign investors have net sold USD 4.88 billion of Indonesian shares so far this year, on track for the largest annual outflow in at least 16 years, and that Goldman Sachs estimates a full MSCI removal could trigger USD 5.6 billion of passive outflows. Lianhe Zaobao says the index has fallen 43% this year and is the world's worst-performing market. Kompas reports that the Indonesia Stock Exchange says the market still qualifies to remain in the emerging-market class under MSCI's standards and was due to meet MSCI on the afternoon of 19 October to seek clarification of the consultation. The rows do not give the date of any MSCI decision, the currency basis of the 43% fall or MSCI's stated reasons, and they give no figures for effects on the real economy or on foreign direct investment.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a market selloff and a consultation, not a reclassification decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a market falling this far, with foreign investors selling, can raise financing costs and weaken the currency, and a move to standalone status would reduce the access of foreign funds to the market. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Indonesia is a construction and manufacturing market in South-East Asia, so higher financing costs or a weaker currency could affect project timing and import prices for chemical inputs, although the rows give no link between the selloff and those sectors. Points that may be worth considering include MSCI's decision timetable, the exchange's talks with MSCI, and moves in the currency and in foreign investment.

Globe and Mail | LiveMint | Lianhe Zaobao | Kompas

item.title: The Bank of Canada's Business Outlook Survey finds sentiment improved in the third quarter, but new US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs weigh on outlooks; many firms expect inflation above 3% for two years, and September inflation was 3.1%.
item.description:
BNN Bloomberg reports that the Bank of Canada's Business Outlook Survey finds sentiment improved on average in the third quarter, but that concerns remain about the Middle East war and rising costs. The survey was conducted mostly before trade talks between Canada and the US broke down at the end of August and Canadian counter-tariffs were announced; after that, companies cited new US tariffs on some goods and counter-tariffs as factors weighing on their outlooks. Inflation expectations have risen with the tariffs and higher energy prices, and the tariffs are weakening outlooks for exports and investment and adding to cost and price pressure. The Financial Post reports that many business leaders expect inflation to stay above 3% for the next two years, that about half of the companies plan to pass on all or some of their cost increases linked to the Iran war and tariffs, and that firms expect non-labour production costs and selling prices to moderate but remain elevated over the next 12 months. MarketScreener reports that Canada's consumer price index rose to 3.1% in September from 3.0%, below the expected monthly rise, and that the Bank of Canada's preferred measures of underlying inflation averaged 1.85%, the slowest in six years. The rows give no sample size, no balance-of-opinion scores and no list of the tariffs or goods concerned.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows combine a survey of business expectations with a consumer price release; the survey was taken mostly before the latest tariffs. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, tariffs that weaken export and investment outlooks while firms pass on costs point to weaker manufacturing and construction demand in Canada and to higher input prices. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Canada is a market for construction and manufacturing products, so lower investment and cost pass-through could reduce volumes and raise price negotiations for suppliers there. The rows give no sector breakdown. Points that may be worth considering include the next Bank of Canada decision, the outcome of US–Canada trade talks, and sector surveys for construction and manufacturing.

BNN Bloomberg | Financial Post | MarketScreener

item.title: Trump says he is open to meeting Putin and Xi but would focus on nuclear arms control, after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin proposed a three-way summit on Ukraine; the Kremlin says no concrete proposals or agenda have been discussed.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that, according to the Wall Street Journal citing a former Russian intelligence officer, Putin proposed a summit with Trump and Xi to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war, with a meeting next month, and that the idea reportedly dates from a Putin–Trump call on 9 October. Commercial Times says the Journal cited informed sources and that the meeting would be at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen; The Standard says the Kremlin put that summit at 18–19 November and that spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no concrete proposals for a meeting or agenda have been discussed, and that no final deal on ending the war can be reached without Kyiv. The Straits Times reports that Trump said he would be willing to meet Putin and Xi but that his focus would be denuclearisation rather than ending the war; it adds that Trump has long pushed for China to join US–Russia arms talks and that Beijing has so far pushed back because its arsenal is much smaller. MarketScreener reports he said he is open to three-way arms-control talks as soon as November, and adds that such a meeting could raise concern in Europe and Asia about private deals, while a deal could also lower global tensions. The rows give no confirmation from Beijing of attendance, no agenda agreed by the three sides and no position from Kyiv or the EU on the proposal.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a proposal and an expression of interest, not a scheduled meeting. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a leaders' meeting would be a diplomatic event with an uncertain outcome; one focused on nuclear arms would not by itself change sanctions, energy flows or trade measures, while a meeting aimed at ending the Ukraine war could affect energy prices, sanctions and European security planning. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, energy and feedstock costs, trade measures towards Russia and China, and European demand for construction and industrial goods all depend on how the war and sanctions develop, and the rows give no link between the proposal and any of them. Points that may be worth considering include confirmation of attendance at the Shenzhen summit, the agenda, and the reactions of Kyiv and EU governments.

Handelsblatt | Commercial Times | The Standard | Straits Times | MarketScreener

item.title: WTO head Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala warns the wars will leave a lasting imprint on trade flows; the WTO forecasts Middle East exports down 17% and imports down 15% this year, and firms may keep the alternative routes and suppliers they have built.
item.description:
Business Recorder reports that WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has warned that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East will leave a lasting imprint on global trade flows. It says the Iran war has sharply contracted Middle Eastern trade, with the WTO forecasting a 17% decline in regional exports and a 15% fall in imports this year. According to the row, even if hostilities end and the Strait of Hormuz reopens, pre-war trade patterns may not return, because businesses may retain the alternative routes and suppliers in which they have invested to hedge against future disruption. This is the only row on the statement. It does not say when or where the Director-General spoke, which countries the Middle East forecast covers, the base year for the 17% and 15% declines, or which products or routes are most affected.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives a warning and two regional forecast figures, not measured trade data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, if firms keep alternative routes and suppliers after the wars, trade patterns would be reordered for longer than the disruption itself, and costs of dual sourcing would remain in prices. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, if chemical and raw-material buyers have adopted alternative routes and suppliers, these could stay in place, which would affect where inputs are bought and what freight and inventory they require, and the forecast 17% decline in Middle East exports could reduce the availability of some inputs from the region if it covers chemical products, although the row names no products. Points that may be worth considering include the next WTO trade forecast, whether Gulf shipping normalises, and which sourcing changes persist.

Business Recorder

item.title: China's commerce ministry and customs announced on 19 October licence-based export controls from 18 November on tunnel-boring machines, certain excavators, wet shotcrete machines and revised dredger-part rules; India says it will consult stakeholders.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports that China's Ministry of Commerce announced on 19 October new export controls on key machinery, including tunnel boring machines, walking excavators and plateau-type wet shotcrete machines, plus optimised controls on dredger items such as slurry pumps, dragheads and cutterheads that meet specified technical thresholds; they take effect on 18 November, exporters must obtain licences and provide detailed technical information, and the stated aim is safeguarding national security and interests. Commercial Times says it is the first time such controls apply to equipment such as shield machines and says the Ministry of Commerce cites non-proliferation among its stated aims. Yahoo Taiwan describes the scope as shield machines, rock tunnel boring machines, their key components and related technologies, walking excavators with strong complex-terrain capability and wet sprayers suited to high altitude, and says the controls cover dual-use items. Xinhua reports that the same day the ministry, customs and the Central Military Commission's equipment development department announced adjusted controls on drone-related items, also from 18 November, which a commerce ministry spokesperson, quoted by Xinhua, describes as dual-use; the South China Morning Post says the licensing-exemption payload threshold rises to 80 litres from 20 and that analysts say the changes could simplify overseas sales of consumer drones but increase compliance costs and delivery times for industrial models. The Economic Times separately reports that India will consult stakeholders, has a scheme to encourage domestic manufacture of such equipment close to final approval, and that Indian officials expect no significant slowdown in highway building. The rows give no trade values, no destination list, no processing times for licences and no share of global supply.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a licensing requirement that starts on 18 November and has not yet been applied. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a licence with detailed technical information adds approval time and uncertainty to exports of tunnelling and earthmoving equipment, which could delay projects abroad that depend on Chinese-made machines and push buyers to other suppliers or to local production. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, tunnelling and infrastructure projects use adhesive technologies and construction chemicals, so delays or supplier changes in equipment could shift the timing of those projects and of demand for construction chemicals, while Chinese machinery makers are themselves customers for adhesive technologies. The rows give no figure for affected projects. Points that may be worth considering include how quickly licences are issued after 18 November, which destinations are affected, and whether other countries respond or the list is extended.

Economic Times, China curbs | Commercial Times | Yahoo Taiwan | South China Morning Post | Xinhua | Economic Times, India response

item.title: The German government signed a letter of intent with Nvidia to advance AI-controlled robots, within an industrial-AI cooperation aimed at small and medium-sized firms; media reports say the government plans a three-digit million amount in support.
item.description:
Wirtschafts Woche reports that the federal economics and research ministries signed a letter of intent with Nvidia to advance the development of AI-controlled robots, that Nvidia will expand cooperation with German partners and make its AI models accessible, in the future, to small and medium-sized firms and research institutions, and that, according to media reports, the government plans to support the project with a three-digit million amount, partly to rent computing capacity in Deutsche Telekom's AI cloud. Wallstreet:online reports that Chancellor Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang affirmed the cooperation on the sidelines of the Invest in Germany summit, with the aim of speeding up the digital transformation of German industry, especially small and medium-sized firms, and securing technological sovereignty. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung says Huang urged Merz to release the political brakes on Germany's economy and warned that if the country does not link its manufacturing strengths with AI, industry will first lose its connection and then its traditional markets. LiveMint says Huang urged German makers of cars and industrial machines to adopt AI and that European leaders are concerned about dependence on US technology companies. The rows give no currency or period for the funding, no list of German companies, no scope of the robotics work and no timetable.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a letter of intent and a reported funding plan, not a funded programme. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, state-backed access to AI models and computing could speed adoption of AI-controlled automation among smaller manufacturers, while LiveMint says European leaders are concerned about the extent of European dependence on US technology companies. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, robots and electronics use adhesive technologies and thermal-management materials, and AI-driven production can raise quality and traceability requirements for suppliers, though the rows give no link between this project and those materials. Points that may be worth considering include the final agreement and its funding, which German firms join, and how sovereignty goals are reconciled with the choice of a US supplier.

Wirtschafts Woche | Wallstreet:online | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | LiveMint

item.title: The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung says direct investment into Germany was EUR 42.7 billion in January–August, one of the lowest for the period in a decade, as the government holds a two-day summit to attract investors.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that the German government is holding an investment summit on Monday and Tuesday in Berlin, attended by the Chancellor and six ministers, with guests including Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Amundi's Valérie Baudson. It says only EUR 42.7 billion in direct investment flowed into Germany from January to August, one of the lowest figures in the last decade for a comparable period, and gives Eli Lilly halving its investment plans because of the government's health reforms as a recent example of waning investor confidence. Handelsblatt reports that Roche is putting all future investments in Germany on hold for the time being because of the federal government's austerity policy in healthcare, while decisions already taken, such as an expansion in Penzberg of more than EUR 600 million, are not affected. Frankfurter Rundschau says the health reform raises the statutory manufacturer discount for many patent-protected medicines from 7% to 15.5% from January 2027. Handelsblatt adds that the government is spending many billions on credit in the coming years to bring infrastructure up to date, a key driver of higher growth this year, though economists warn that a sustainable recovery has yet to be achieved. The rows name two companies and do not show a wider pattern; they give no baseline year for the 42.7 billion and no pledges from the summit.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe an investor-outreach event and a flow figure whose baseline they do not give, not investment decisions. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, weak foreign direct investment can mean fewer new plants and expansions in Germany, while credit-financed infrastructure spending supports construction demand if projects start. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new plants and infrastructure use construction and industrial adhesive technologies, so investment announcements that turn into projects would raise demand with a lag, while postponed investment lowers it. The rows give no investment figures for the chemical industry. Points that may be worth considering include pledges announced at the summit, later direct investment data, and whether other sectors than pharmaceuticals report postponements.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Handelsblatt, Roche | Frankfurter Rundschau, Roche | Handelsblatt, government borrowing

item.title: Wallstreet:online reports Redfin data showing nearly 45% of US sellers made concessions in August, and that Lennar's housing gross margin fell to 15.8%, its lowest since 2008/09, with new orders down 9%.
item.description:
Wallstreet:online reports that US mortgage rates of over 7% are deterring buyers and that more homeowners are lowering asking prices. According to Redfin, nearly 45% of home sellers made financial concessions to buyers in August, and about 70% in particularly weak markets such as Atlanta and Nashville; in the four weeks to 20 September, 21% of sellers reduced listing prices. The row says new-build providers are advertising with high discounts and preferential financing. At Lennar, it reports, the average selling price fell from USD 383,000 to USD 372,000 in the third fiscal quarter, discounts averaged the equivalent of 12% of the price, the gross margin in housing construction shrank to 15.8%, the lowest since the 2008/09 financial crisis, and new orders fell by 9%. The row names Lennar and KB Home as large US builders under pressure but gives figures only for Lennar. It does not give the comparison period for the 9% fall in orders or the margin a year earlier, and it does not say whether the USD 383,000 is the prior quarter or the prior year.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row combines Redfin-reported seller behaviour with one builder's quarterly results, so it describes pressure on pricing and margins more than on building volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, builders that cut prices and lose margin tend to slow starts and to press suppliers on cost, and high mortgage rates reduce the pool of buyers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new housing uses adhesive technologies in insulation, flooring and facades, so weaker builder orders and margins could lower demand from US residential construction and increase price pressure on suppliers. The row gives no figures for housing starts. Points that may be worth considering include other builders' quarterly results, mortgage-rate moves, and starts and permits data.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: The Chemical Industries Association's third-quarter survey forecasts UK chemical production down 2.4% in 2026, against 0.6% in the EU and broadly flat in the US, and down a further 7.1% in the fourth quarter.
item.description:
The Chemical Industries Association (CIA) says its third-quarter 2026 business survey shows the UK chemical industry facing a deepening competitiveness crisis. It forecasts UK chemical production to fall by 2.4% in 2026 and to contract by a further 7.1% in the fourth quarter of 2026. It describes the UK as the weakest-performing chemical producer among the major economies compared: production in the EU is expected to decline by just 0.6%, and US production is described as broadly flat. On the main challenges, 52% of businesses name energy costs as their single biggest challenge, 21% name weakening demand and 12% name raw material costs. The association's release is the only row on the survey, so the figures are the association's own. The row does not give the number of firms surveyed, the base for the 7.1% fourth-quarter figure, whether the 2.4% and 0.6% are calendar-year changes on the same base, or any figures by product group, prices or orders.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row describes a trade association's survey and forecasts, not official output statistics. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling chemical output with energy named as the main burden points to weaker domestic supply and to cost pressure that producers may pass on to customers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chemical producers can supply resins, polymers and other inputs, so lower output or energy-driven price rises could affect the availability and cost of raw materials for adhesive technologies products made in or supplied to the UK, while weaker UK manufacturing demand would lower sales of those products there. The row gives no figures for specific raw materials or for UK adhesive output. Points that may be worth considering include whether the fourth-quarter forecast is revised, how UK and EU energy costs compare, and whether other European chemical associations report a similar gap.

Chemical Industries Association

item.title: Ifo finds German industry had 496,000 fewer jobs subject to social security contributions at the end of 2025 than at the start of 2019, a 7.1% fall, with carmakers and suppliers, metal products and machinery accounting for 303,600 of the loss.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that a study published by the Ifo Institute finds German industry has lost nearly 500,000 jobs subject to social security contributions since 2019, partly due to growing competition from China: at the end of 2025, 496,000 fewer people worked there than at the beginning of 2019, a decrease of 7.1%. In the same period the service sector created over 2.2 million new jobs, mainly in health and social services and public administration. All federal states except Hamburg are affected; the decline is 8.4% in the East and 6.8% in the West, and in East Germany new jobs in car manufacturing were created only in Brandenburg, thanks to the Tesla plant. Daily Sabah gives the sector split: 123,500 jobs lost across carmakers and suppliers, a fall of 13%, 115,600 in metal businesses and 64,500 in machinery; Dünya adds that these three sectors total 303,600, about 61% of the decline. Frankfurter Rundschau cites the Federal Statistical Office as saying larger industrial companies employed about 144,100 fewer people at the end of June 2026 than a year earlier, 42,300 of them in the automotive industry. The rows give no figures for chemicals or for output, and they do not reconcile the Ifo and Federal Statistical Office bases.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe job counts, not output or orders, and the Ifo figure covers employment subject to social security contributions while the Federal Statistical Office figure covers larger industrial firms over a different period, so the two are not additive. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a smaller industrial workforce lowers demand for the materials and services industry buys, and losses concentrated in vehicles, metals and machinery point to weaker demand from those customer groups. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle, metal-product and machinery makers use adhesive technologies, so falling employment there can accompany lower production and lower consumption, although the rows give no production data. Points that may be worth considering include later Ifo and Federal Statistical Office employment figures, output indicators for the three sectors, and the gap between East and West.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Daily Sabah | Dünya Gazetesi | Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: The Guardian reports that China's property investment fell 20.6% in the first nine months of 2026; Chinatimes reports that the 70-city house price index fell 2.8% year on year in September, the slowest decline in 2026.
item.description:
The Guardian reports that China's fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months of 2026, that property investment fell by 20.6% and that infrastructure spending remained weak. Chinatimes, citing the National Bureau of Statistics, reports that in September 2026 the house price index of 70 large and medium-sized cities declined by 2.8% year on year and by 0.1% from August, the slowest decline in 2026. It gives new-home price changes by city tier: first-tier cities down 0.5% year on year, with Beijing down 2.7%, Guangzhou down 1.1% and Shenzhen down 1.0% while Shanghai rose 2.8%; second-tier cities down 2.4%; third-tier cities down 3.9%. A second Chinatimes row says that from August, new-home prices rose 0.2% in Shanghai and Guangzhou and 0.3% in Shenzhen, fell 0.2% in Beijing, and were flat in second-tier cities after a 0.1% fall in August. The Guardian row does not state the comparison period for the 20.6% and gives no figures for floor space, sales or construction starts. The Chinatimes rows do not say how the 70-city index is weighted.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows combine an investment total with price indices; neither measures construction activity, completions or sales volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall in property investment of that size lowers new building and the volume of materials used in it, while a slowing price decline can indicate that the market is closer to stabilising without showing a recovery in building. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, residential building and fit-out use adhesive technologies, so lower property investment points to lower demand from that end market in China, while renovation and existing-home activity could take a larger share. The rows give no figures for floor space, starts or completions. Points that may be worth considering include whether the investment decline narrows in the next monthly release, how prices in second- and third-tier cities develop, and whether sales and starts data show the same pattern.

The Guardian | Chinatimes, 70-city index | Chinatimes, month-on-month changes

item.title: A Jefferies report says global container freight rates have risen 130% since February 2026 because of Middle East tensions; the Economic Times adds that India's container trade value rose 23% year on year in September.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports a Jefferies report finding that global container freight rates have risen by 130% since February 2026 due to the impact of Middle East tensions. In the same article, it says India's container-based export-import trade grew strongly in September 2026: trade value rose 23% year on year, with exports up 22% and imports up 23%. Exports to the United States grew significantly, while those to the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia fell. Dawn, in a separate article, says the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait came under renewed threat after the US attack on Iran on 28 February 2026, that partial maritime traffic through Hormuz has reportedly resumed, and that Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb is a concern for Saudi Arabia. The Economic Times row does not give the freight index or the routes behind the 130%, the rate level in February or now, or whether it refers to spot or contract rates. It gives no volumes for India's trade and no size for the declines in exports to the Gulf.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give one Jefferies report's figure for the change in container rates since February, without the underlying index. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rise of that size raises the landed cost of imported goods, can lengthen delivery times, and reaches industries that import raw materials or ship finished goods in containers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, specialty chemicals and additives can move in containers, so higher freight rates could raise the delivered cost of imported inputs and of exports to distant markets, with the effect depending on the value of the cargo in each container. The rows give no figure for chemical shipments or for particular trade lanes. Points that may be worth considering include which index underlies the 130%, whether rates ease if Gulf shipping normalises, and how freight cost compares with cargo value on key lanes.

Economic Times | Dawn
